summary: Propranolol is a lipophilic, non-selective beta-blocker used for hypertension, angina, rate control in atrial fibrillation, post-MI secondary prevention, migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, hypertrophic subaortic stenosis, and pheochromocytoma (adjunctive). It undergoes high hepatic first-pass metabolism (~25% bioavailability) via CYP2D6, 1A2 and 2C19. Doses must be individualized due to variable bioavailability, and therapy must never be stopped abruptly to avoid rebound angina, MI, or thyrotoxicosis exacerbation.
indications: Hypertension (alone or with a thiazide diuretic)
Angina pectoris due to coronary atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation - control of rapid ventricular rate
Reduction of cardiovascular mortality after acute myocardial infarction in clinically stable patients
Hypertrophic subaortic stenosis - improvement of NYHA functional class

moa: Non-selective competitive antagonist at beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors with no intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. Blockade reduces heart rate, myocardial contractility and cardiac output, inhibits renin release, and reduces sympathetic outflow, lowering blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand. At high concentrations it has a quinidine-like membrane-stabilising action. Antimigraine and antitremor effects are not fully established but may involve central and beta-2 mechanisms.

absolute: Sinus bradycardia and greater than first-degree AV block

preg: No adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Crosses the placenta; intrauterine growth retardation, small placentas and congenital abnormalities reported, and neonates exposed at parturition have shown bradycardia, hypoglycemia and/or respiratory depression. Use only if potential benefit justifies risk to the fetus; ensure neonatal monitoring at birth.
lact: Propranolol is excreted in human milk. Exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman; observe the infant for bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycemia.
renal: Use with caution. In chronic renal failure peak plasma concentrations may be 3-4 times higher and metabolite levels up to 3 times higher despite a shorter plasma half-life. Propranolol is not significantly dialyzable. Hypoglycemia has been reported in patients with renal insufficiency.
hepatic: Extensively metabolized by the liver; use with caution. In cirrhosis steady-state unbound concentration increased ~3-fold and half-life rose from ~4 to ~11 hours. Reduce dose and titrate carefully.

major: Quinidine (raises propranolol levels 2-3x, greater beta-blockade, postural hypotension)
Verapamil / diltiazem and other negative-inotropic calcium channel blockers (bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, heart failure)
Digitalis glycosides (additive AV nodal slowing, bradycardia)
Reserpine / catecholamine-depleting agents (marked bradycardia, hypotension, syncope)
Epinephrine (unopposed alpha effect - severe hypertension; not for propranolol overdose)
Clonidine (beta-blockers antagonize antihypertensive effect; rebound on clonidine withdrawal)
moderate: CYP2D6 inhibitors - fluoxetine, paroxetine, cimetidine, ritonavir (raise propranolol levels)
CYP1A2 inhibitors - fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin, theophylline (raise propranolol levels)
CYP2C19 inhibitors - fluconazole, fluvoxamine (raise propranolol levels)
Warfarin (increased bioavailability and prothrombin time - monitor INR)
Thioridazine / chlorpromazine (increased levels of both drugs)
MAO inhibitors / tricyclic antidepressants (altered hypotensive effects)
Rifampin, phenytoin, phenobarbital, smoking (induce metabolism, lower levels)
minor: Cholestyramine / colestipol (reduce propranolol absorption up to 50%)
Lovastatin / pravastatin (mutual AUC reduction 18-23%, no PD change)
interactions.food: Protein-rich foods increase propranolol bioavailability by about 50% without changing time to peak; take consistently with respect to meals.
interactions.alcohol: Concomitant alcohol may increase plasma levels of propranolol; avoid.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise serum potassium, transaminases and alkaline phosphatase; alters thyroid tests (increases T4 and reverse T3, decreases T3); may interfere with glaucoma screening (lowers intraocular pressure); may reduce sensitivity of dobutamine stress echocardiography.

rare: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, exfoliative dermatitis, erythema multiforme
emergency: Severe bronchospasm / laryngospasm with respiratory distress
Severe symptomatic bradycardia or high-degree heart block

monitoring: Heart rate and blood pressure at baseline and after dose changes
Signs and symptoms of heart failure
Blood glucose in diabetic or fasting/at-risk patients (masked hypoglycemia)
Thyroid function and symptoms when used in/near hyperthyroidism
INR / prothrombin time if on warfarin
Serum potassium, transaminases and alkaline phosphatase in hypertensive patients
Exercise tolerance and ECG ischemic changes in angina
counsel: Do not stop the medication suddenly; abrupt withdrawal can cause chest pain, heart attack or worsened tremor/thyroid symptoms
Take consistently with respect to food
Report shortness of breath, swelling, very slow pulse, wheezing or fainting
Diabetics: be aware that warning signs of low blood sugar (fast heartbeat) may be masked
Rise slowly to avoid dizziness; avoid alcohol
Tell clinicians you take a beta-blocker before surgery or allergy testing
It may take days to weeks to see full benefit for blood pressure or migraine
pk: Antihypertensive effect over days to weeks; acute beta-blockade within ~1-2 h
Plasma peak ~1-4 hours after oral dose
3-6 hours (up to ~11 h in elderly and cirrhosis)
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light; tight, light-resistant container
pearls: Lipophilic - crosses the blood-brain barrier, useful for migraine, tremor and anxiety-related somatic symptoms
Non-selective beta-2 blockade makes it unsuitable in asthma and risky in COPD
In pheochromocytoma never give before adequate alpha-blockade to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction
Glucagon (50-150 mcg/kg IV then 1-5 mg/h) is the antidote for refractory beta-blocker toxicity; epinephrine is contraindicated
Only ~25% reaches systemic circulation due to high first-pass metabolism - explains wide interindividual dose variability
Masks hyperthyroid signs and can precipitate thyroid storm if stopped abruptly
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule - do not double up. Avoid letting doses lapse, as interrupting therapy can trigger rebound angina or hypertension.
overdose: Hypotension and bradycardia are typical and treated supportively; bronchospasm and depressed myocardial function may occur. Evacuate recent gastric contents protecting the airway. Glucagon 50-150 mcg/kg IV followed by 1-5 mg/hour infusion is particularly useful for hypotension/depressed contractility. Atropine or isoproterenol for bradycardia; temporary pacing for serious bradycardia; isoproterenol or aminophylline for bronchospasm. Isoproterenol, dopamine or phosphodiesterase inhibitors may help; epinephrine may cause uncontrolled hypertension and should be avoided. Propranolol is not significantly dialyzable.
